unit.title: The Little Words That Sound Native
unit.subtitle: Pragmatic markers and discourse fillers: pues, o sea, vamos, hombre, en plan

grammar.title: Muletillas: the glue of spoken Spanish
grammar.intro: The gap between correct Spanish and native Spanish is often a handful of tiny words that carry almost no dictionary meaning but do enormous pragmatic work: they hedge, emphasize, buy thinking time, manage turns and signal your stance. Master pues, o sea, vamos, hombre, en plan and the rest, and your speech stops sounding translated. These are spoken and informal — save them for conversation, not formal writing.

sections.heading: Fillers and reformulators
sections.body: Some markers mainly fill space or repackage what you just said. Pues opens a turn and buys a beat (“well…”). O sea reformulates or clarifies (“I mean / that is”), and among younger speakers it also hedges. En plan is the newer quotative/approximator (“like…”), introducing an example, a manner or reported speech. Bueno concedes, backtracks or changes topic.

ex.es: —¿Vienes? —Pues no sé, depende de la hora.
ex.en: —Coming? —Well, I dunno, depends on the time.
ex.note: pues opens the reply and stalls

ex.es: Me miró en plan “¿y tú quién eres?”.
ex.en: She looked at me like, “and who are you?”

sections.heading: Emphasis, appeal and softening
sections.body: Other markers colour the whole utterance. Vamos and pero vamos reinforce or sum up a stance (“I mean, really / to be honest”). Hombre and mujer (used to anyone, regardless of gender in many regions) appeal to the listener — surprise, mild protest or warmth (“come on / oh come now”). Venga urges, agrees or closes (“come on / all right then”). Digamos hedges an approximate word choice (“let's say”).
conj: come on / all right then (urges, closes)

ex.es: No es tonto, hombre, solo está despistado.
ex.en: He's not stupid, come on, he's just distracted.
ex.note: hombre = mild protest, appeal to listener

ex.es: Venga, nos vemos mañana y lo hablamos.
ex.en: All right, see you tomorrow and we'll talk it over.

sections.heading: ya, mira, oye and emphatic si
sections.body: A final cluster manages attention and stance. Mira and oye grab the floor or flag what follows (“look… / hey, listen…”), oye often introducing a new topic or a favour. Ya signals understanding or (with irony) disbelief (“right / yeah, sure”). Emphatic si at the start of a clause — written without an accent, unlike conditional si and affirmative sí — protests or justifies: ¡Si no lo sabía! = “But I didn't even know!”.

ex.es: Oye, ¿te importaría echarme una mano con esto?
ex.en: Hey, would you mind giving me a hand with this?

ex.es: —Te lo dije. —¡Si yo no estaba allí!
ex.en: —I told you. —But I wasn't even there!

takeaways: pues stalls and opens a turn; o sea reformulates; en plan approximates or quotes (“like”).
vamos / pero vamos reinforce a stance; digamos hedges a wording.
hombre / mujer appeal to the listener; venga urges, agrees or closes.
Emphatic si (no accent) protests or justifies: ¡Si no lo sabía!

mistakes.w: Sí no lo sabía, ¿por qué me culpas?
mistakes.r: ¡Si no lo sabía! ¿Por qué me culpas?
mistakes.why: Emphatic protesting si takes no accent; sí (with accent) would mean the affirmative 'yes'.

mistakes.w: No estoy enfadado, mujer… bien, un poco.
mistakes.r: No estoy enfadado, mujer… bueno, un poco.
mistakes.why: To concede or backtrack you need bueno; bien means 'well/fine' in the manner sense, not the discourse marker.

mistakes.w: Era, como plan, muy raro todo.
mistakes.r: Era, en plan, muy raro todo.
mistakes.why: The colloquial approximator is the fixed phrase en plan, not 'como plan'.

exercises.prompt: —Te avisé ayer. —¡___ yo no estaba en casa!
exercises.prompt_en: —I warned you yesterday. —But I wasn't even home!
exercises.ok: ¡Exacto! El si enfático de protesta va sin tilde.
exercises.no: The emphatic protest is “si” without an accent; “sí” would be the affirmative 'yes'.

exercises.prompt: No me cae mal, ___, es que no lo conozco mucho.
exercises.prompt_en: I don't dislike him, I mean, it's just that I don't know him well.
exercises.no: To reformulate/clarify you use “o sea” (I mean). The other forms change the meaning or are ungrammatical here.

exercises.prompt: Build: “Hey, would you mind giving me a hand with this?”
exercises.ok: ¡Perfecto! Oye abre la petición con naturalidad.
exercises.no: Open the favour with “Oye” and keep the polite conditional “importaría”.

exercises.prompt: No es tonto, ___, solo está un poco despistado.
exercises.prompt_en: He's not stupid, come on, he's just a bit distracted.
exercises.hint: An appeal to the listener — a mild 'come on' that isn't gender-bound.
exercises.no: The appeal marker here is “hombre” (a mild 'come on' addressed to the listener).

exercises.prompt: Match each marker to its pragmatic function.

exercises.tts: Pues no sé, o sea, depende de cómo lo mires.
accepted: pues no se, o sea, depende de como lo mires
exercises.translation: Well, I dunno, I mean, it depends how you look at it.
exercises.ok: ¡Correcto! “Pues no sé, o sea, depende de cómo lo mires.”
exercises.no: It was: “Pues no sé, o sea, depende de cómo lo mires.” (two fillers stacked, very colloquial).

exercises.scenario: A friend is beating himself up over a tiny mistake 😅

lines.speaker: Marta
lines.es: Soy un desastre, lo he hecho fatal, no sirvo para esto.
lines.en: I'm a disaster, I did it terribly, I'm no good at this.

options.text: Hombre, no exageres, que ha sido solo un fallo tonto.
Sí, tienes toda la razón, eres un desastre absoluto.
Vaya, en plan desastre total, digamos que sí.

exercises.ok: ¡Perfecto! Hombre + no exageres reconforta y quita hierro.
exercises.no: The warm, reassuring reply opens with “Hombre, no exageres…”. The others agree with the self-criticism or misuse the fillers.

exercises.say: Pues no sé, o sea, ya veremos.
exercises.en: Well, I dunno, I mean, we'll see.
exercises.no: Almost — tap “Hear it” and let pues and o sea flow casually, without pausing on them.
